facts.text: I discussed bisphenol-A (BPA) as a chemical with hormone-like behavior that has been associated with health issues.
BPA is a component of polycarbonate plastic.
BPA is used as an additive in some epoxy resins and other materials.
BPA has been removed or substituted in many cases, especially in water bottles and baby bottles.
A long review by the European Food Safety Agency (EFSA) was mentioned as reinforcing concerns and findings.
The EFSA review concluded that BPA has the potential to cause harm at high levels, but most exposures are so low that risks are negligible based on current understanding.
The discussion focused on BPA exposure from contaminated food as the most relevant source of exposure in most studies.
Ingested BPA is not readily absorbed from the gut.
When ingested, BPA is rapidly converted (metabolized) into a less harmful form and removed in healthy adults.
BPA can potentially get into the body through the skin.
A team at the University of Missouri was particularly interested in BPA exposure through skin.
BPA is used as a developer for heat-sensitive ink in many cash register receipts that use thermal paper.
BPA is applied as a surface coating on thermal paper receipts.
BPA can potentially transfer from receipts to hands during handling.
The study tested whether hand sanitizer could dissolve BPA from receipts and enhance absorption through the skin.
The study measured BPA present in cash register receipts from local retailers.
The study found an average of 20 mg of BPA per receipt in receipts that used BPA.
The study found that BPA was 2% of the weight of those receipts.
The study tested volunteers with dry hands handling receipts for different lengths of time up to 6 minutes.
After 6 minutes of handling a receipt with dry hands, an average of 7 µg of BPA ended up on a person’s hand.
After 6 minutes, the 7 µg of BPA on the hand was about 0.08% of the BPA on the receipt.
The study tested what happened when hands were coated with Purell and a receipt was held without allowing the sanitizer to dry.
With Purell-coated wet hands, the study found a maximum of 600 µg of BPA transferred after one minute.
With Purell-coated wet hands, about 7% of the BPA on the receipt ended up on the hand after one minute.
The study measured how much BPA passed through the skin and into the bloodstream.
Volunteers held a BPA-coated receipt for four minutes with the BPA-coated side in contact with the hand.
Blood samples were taken for 90 minutes.
The analysis looked at free (unconjugated) BPA in blood.
The analysis looked at conjugated BPA in blood.
The study had volunteers eat 10 french fries from their Purell and BPA-coated hands.
The study found measurable quantities of unconjugated BPA enter the bloodstream within minutes after holding a BPA-containing receipt for 4 minutes with a Purell-coated hand.
The peak blood concentration of unconjugated BPA was 5.7 nanograms per milliliter for males.
The peak blood concentration of unconjugated BPA was 10.2 nanograms per milliliter for females.
For females, the discussion stated that around ten billionths of a blood sample would be BPA at the peak concentration.
For volunteers who did not use Purell, there was no measurable increase in BPA in their blood.
The discussion suggested most BPA found in blood samples was from the skin rather than from transferred BPA entering the gut.
The discussion speculated that BPA on the fries could have passed into the bloodstream through the inside of the mouth.
The discussion stated that the combination of hand sanitizer and BPA-containing cash register receipts can lead to elevated levels of unconjugated BPA in the blood stream.
The discussion stated that handling receipts with clean, dry hands is unlikely to lead to significant transfer of BPA from receipts to the blood.
The discussion said the Purell exposure scenarios were not realistic for most people.
The discussion said holding receipts in Purell-coated hands with the printed side palm-down for up to four minutes was not likely to be routine.
The discussion said the measured blood levels are peak levels from one-off events and are small.
The discussion said risk interpretation would require information about how often such events occur over a day.
The discussion emphasized that dose over time matters more than a one-off peak.
The discussion said unconjugated BPA levels were relatively high compared to conjugated BPA.
The discussion suggested unconjugated BPA may be higher because BPA passes through the skin and enters the bloodstream before passing through the liver.
The discussion stated that the authors suggested increased risk to sensitive organs and systems, but that this remains speculative without further research.
The discussion concluded that the speaker would not change cash register receipt habits.
The discussion suggested that smothering hands with Purell and clutching receipts for several minutes probably isn’t advisable.
The discussion specifically warned against doing this especially if about to eat french fries.
